doc.title: Bobby Shew interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 1, 2020

title: Clinical music teaching and uptight orchestras
summary: Shew complains that lessons drill players not to miss notes, with the emotion lost, and that orchestras under conductors like Ozawa are tense.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: You had shared a little lesson that I’d like to hear about again, and that was getting your students to play an F scale —

Oh yeah. Well the thing is, here’s the bottom line for me and what I was delving into, and I’m sorry you’d know that I kissed the Blarney stone at one time you know, I have this gabbing kind of gift that I keep going. But I take these asides in conversation quite often. But the thing about it that I was getting at is that music is basically an emotional thing. It’s not supposed to be just a clinical, don’t-miss-a-note kind of thing. And that’s what’s happened to music education over the years to a point where you know you sit in and — you take a lesson. What are you doing? The guy makes you play a page until you don’t miss a note on it. Well you miss the whole point of why are you playing it, where’s the emotion? Where’s the joy? Where’s the humanity of this, the real meaning behind music. You know? It’s not even there. And most of the teachers are not even aware of it because it’s like the contagion of aberration they call it, it’s one generation after another keep passing on, you know, kind of an attitude about music and you get into a concert band and the band director’s just, oh we’ll play this until we don’t miss any notes. Then you get in an orchestra and how uptight is that? A guy like Ozawa in front of an orchestra for Christ’s sake, everybody’s like dropping Valiums every ten minutes, you notice that?
Yes. I’ve often wondered why nobody in an orchestra seems to ever smile.
